Note: S0881's Step 23, revisiting the sufficiency/readiness/completeness theme first opened in Step 13 (S0867) with much heavier mathematical formalization: the EpistemicContract as the Knowledge-to-Action bridge, three separated readiness levels, Knowledge Boundary/Frontier, EpistemicGap and Epistemic Debt, KnowledgeOS Goal=max Utility(K,P) not max|K|, and S1-S16 invariants; this file's own closing section proposes Step 24, which the batch already processed as S0880.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Given multiple pieces of evidence, how can KnowledgeOS combine them into an assessment without double-counting, losing uncertainty, or manufacturing certainty? I will deliberately not choose Bayesian probability, Dempster–Shafer, fuzzy logic, weighted scoring, or another framework yet. First we deri
a_rows_sample.statement: States the governing method for Step 25C: derive required algebraic properties for evidence aggregation before selecting any specific mathematical framework.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.1 — Start with the simplest case ... Assess(H,E_1)=0.8. Why? Because the number 0.8 has no defined semantics. Does it mean 80% probability that H is true? 80% confidence? 80% source reliability? 80% evidence strength? 80% decision readiness? These are different things. No numerical value without
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms the rule 'no numerical value without defined semantics' — a bare 0.8 could mean five different incompatible things.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.2 — Separate the dimensions ... Assessment(H,E) = (R,D,T,A,I,C,U) where relevance; directness; temporal fit; authenticity; independence; consistency; uncertainty. This is not yet the final structure. It is an experimental decomposition. ... 25C.3 — Evidence support relation ... Supports(E,H) and
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a seven-dimension Assessment tuple (Relevance,Directness,TemporalFit,Authenticity,Independence,Consistency,Uncertainty) and a four-valued qualitative Support relation {Support,Challenge,Neutral,Unknown}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.4 — Experiment A: duplicate evidence ... byte-for-byte identical copies. Aggregate(E_1,E_1,H) = Aggregate(E_1,H) in semantic effect. Idempotency x\oplus x=x for semantically duplicate evidence.
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives the first algebraic requirement, Idempotency x⊕x=x, from a duplicate-evidence thought experiment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.5 — Experiment B: independent corroboration ... E_1 direct infrastructure query. E_2 independent backup-system query. Both support H. these should provide additional information. x\oplus y\neq x when x and y are genuinely independent information. Evidence identity and evidence independence are d
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows independent (non-duplicate) evidence must genuinely increase support (x⊕y≠x), establishing Evidence identity and Evidence independence are different concepts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.6 — Experiment C: dependent evidence ... E_1 Vendor documentation says X. E_2 Internal report copied from vendor documentation. E_2=f(E_1). Counting both as independent evidence creates false certainty. Therefore the algebra needs a dependency relation Dep(E_2,E_1). The effective independent inf
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires an explicit Dep(E2,E1) dependency relation for copied evidence, reducing effective independent information to {E1} rather than {E1,E2}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.7 — Experiment D: contradiction ... E_1\vdash H and E_2\vdash \neg H. A naive weighted average might produce Support(H)=0.5. But that loses critical information. The correct state is Conflict(H) with Support(H)>0 and Challenge(H)>0. Conflict\neq Uncertainty. This is extremely important. ... 25C.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Conflict≠Uncertainty via a three-case taxonomy (no evidence→Unknown; weak one-sided evidence→WeaklySupported; strong both-sided evidence→Conflicted), rejecting a naive weighted average that would collapse contradiction to 0.5.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.9 — Experiment E: stale evidence ... Was H true in 2024? it may be excellent. Is H true today? it may be insufficient. Support(E,H) must be evaluated relative to QuestionTime. We therefore need TemporalFit(E,H,t). ... 25C.10 — Experiment F: evidence reliability ... calibrated monitoring system v
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires TemporalFit(E,H,t) for question-time-relative evidence assessment, and distinguishes Reliability from Relevance (a highly reliable source can still be irrelevant to a specific hypothesis).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.11 — Experiment G: authentic but false ... The backup is verified. The document is authentic. Later the actual restore test fails. Authenticity(E)=High while Support(H) may be reduced by stronger contradictory evidence. Authenticity\neq Correctness. This is another reason the dimensions must rem
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Authenticity from Correctness — an authentic document can still turn out to be factually wrong upon later contradictory evidence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.12 — Experiment H: AI evidence ... We cannot simply give it Reliability=0. That would also be too simplistic. An LLM can produce useful extraction; transformation; interpretation; hypothesis; hallucination. Therefore the system must represent how the AI output was produced. AIOutput \rightarrow
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues AI-produced evidence should not automatically receive Reliability=0 (too simplistic); the system must represent AIOutput→Transformation→SourceArtifact, letting the underlying artifact carry the actual evidential weight.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.13 — Evidence provenance becomes part of aggregation ... E_1 from a source. E_2 is an LLM summary of E_1. E_3 is a human report based on E_2. Naively 3 pieces of evidence. Actually 1 underlying evidence lineage. Aggregation must operate over evidence lineage, not merely evidence count. This is a
a_rows_sample.statement: States the major result that aggregation must operate over evidence lineage (a three-hop derivation chain collapses to one underlying lineage), not merely a count of records.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.14 — Algebraic requirement: commutativity ... E_1,E_2 versus E_2,E_1. The final semantic assessment should normally be identical. E_1\oplus E_2 = E_2\oplus E_1. Commutativity for order-independent evidence aggregation. If order matters, that must be explicitly because of temporal semantics, not
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives the Commutativity requirement (E1⊕E2=E2⊕E1) for order-independent evidence aggregation, with order-dependence permitted only via explicit temporal semantics, never implementation accident.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.15 — Associativity ... (E_1\oplus E_2)\oplus E_3 = E_1\oplus(E_2\oplus E_3). This is associativity. If this fails, distributed computation becomes much harder. ... 25C.16 — But temporal evidence creates a qualification ... Aggregation may need to be evaluated relative to a query time. Aggregate(
a_rows_sample.statement: Derives Associativity as a required property (needed for distributed computation), qualified by making aggregation contextual: Aggregate(E1,E2|QueryContext) with Time/Scope/Goal as context parameters.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.17 — First candidate structure ... \mathcal{E}(H)=(S_H,C_H,U_H,L_H) where supporting evidence lineage; challenging evidence lineage; unresolved/uncertain evidence; dependency/lineage structure. This is intentionally not yet a scalar score. ... 25C.18 — Why this is powerful ... Supported by two i
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a non-scalar aggregated evidence structure E(H)=(S_H,C_H,U_H,L_H) — supporting/challenging lineages, unresolved evidence, dependency structure — argued more epistemically useful than a bare confidence scalar.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.19 — But we eventually need numerical decisions ... Sārathi may need Risk(A_1)<Risk(A_2). Therefore numerical reasoning will eventually be required. But now we can make the correct architectural distinction: Evidence Algebra \rightarrow Assessment Representation \rightarrow Decision Model rather
a_rows_sample.statement: Concedes numerical decision-making is eventually needed but insists on the layered architecture Evidence Algebra→Assessment Representation→Decision Model, never a direct Evidence→OneUniversalScore shortcut.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.20 — Candidate statistical layer ... P(H\mid E). Bayesian updating is attractive because it handles sequential evidence. But P(E_1,E_2\mid H) requires modeling dependencies. If we incorrectly assume P(E_1,E_2\mid H)=P(E_1\mid H)P(E_2\mid H), we may double-count correlated evidence. Therefore Bay
a_rows_sample.statement: Evaluates Bayesian updating: attractive for sequential evidence, but naive conditional independence assumptions double-count correlated evidence — Bayesian math makes the dependency problem explicit rather than eliminating it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.21 — Dempster–Shafer? ... Bel(H) and Pl(H). Bel(H)\neq Pl(H) can represent epistemic uncertainty without forcing a precise probability. But conflict handling and source dependence remain difficult. Candidate, not selected. ... 25C.22 — Fuzzy logic? ... \mu_H(x)\in[0,1] ... FuzzyMembership does n
a_rows_sample.statement: Evaluates Dempster-Shafer (Bel≠Pl useful for uncertainty without forcing precision, but conflict/dependency handling remain difficult) and Fuzzy logic (FuzzyMembership≠Probability, useful for some domains but not universal) — both explicitly marked Candidate, not selected.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.23 — Weighted scoring? ... Score(H)=\sum_iw_i e_i. This is easy to compute. But it has severe problems: weights can be arbitrary; dependence is difficult; conflict can disappear into an average; calibration is unclear; 0.8 has no intrinsic epistemic meaning. Useful engineering heuristic\neq Univ
a_rows_sample.statement: Evaluates weighted scoring, listing five severe problems (arbitrary weights, dependency difficulty, conflict disappearing into averages, unclear calibration, meaningless scalars) — a useful engineering heuristic, never a universal epistemic algebra.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.24 — The result of the comparison ... We therefore should not choose a single universal mathematical framework yet. Instead KnowledgeOS should probably have layers: Evidence Representation ↓ Evidence Dependency/Lineage ↓ Assessment Algebra ↓ Statistical/Logical Inference ↓ Decision Model. Differ
a_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates the comparison result: no single universal framework is chosen; instead a five-layer architecture (Evidence Representation→Dependency/Lineage→Assessment Algebra→Statistical/Logical Inference→Decision Model) allows different bounded contexts to use different inference mechanisms.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 25C.25 — A critical DDD insight ... We should not create a giant KnowledgeConfidenceService that decides everything. Evidence context knows Evidence and Provenance. Assessment context knows Support, Challenge, Reliability, Uncertainty. Statistical context knows Probability, Distribution, Calibration
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a monolithic 'KnowledgeConfidenceService' in favor of four DDD bounded contexts (Evidence, Assessment, Statistical, Decision) each owning distinct concerns, communicating through explicit contracts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E=(Content,Source,Provenance,Method,Time,Context,Reliability,Independence,Authority,Uncertainty) ... 0.87+0.76+0.91 has no generally valid statistical interpretation
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects representing evidence as a bare scalar confidence summed across items (0.87+0.76+0.91 has no valid statistical interpretation), proposing instead a ten-field Evidence tuple E=(Content,Source,Provenance,Method,Time,Context,Reliability,Independence,Authority,Uncertainty), not all fields required per domain.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Support, Reliability, Authority, Probability, Confidence, Independence ... they answer different questions
b_rows_sample.statement: States six concepts that must remain separate: Support, Reliability, Authority, Probability, Confidence, Independence — each answers a different question.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Support(E,A) ... Supports/Contradicts/Neutral/Undetermined ... can be deterministic
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Support(E,A) with four possible values (Supports, Contradicts, Neutral, Undetermined), potentially deterministic.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reliability(E,A,C) ... Production API high reliability for current version, Human memory low reliability for exact historical version ... context-dependent
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Reliability(E,A,C) as context-dependent trustworthiness of a source/method for a specific claim type, illustrated with production-API-vs-human-memory example.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A production server may be authoritative for CurrentInstalledVersion ... an Architecture Board ... ArchitectureApproval ... Authority\neq Reliability
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Authority as organizational/legal standing to establish or approve an assertion, distinct from Reliability, worked with a production-server-vs-Architecture-Board example.

b_rows_sample.anchor: An engineer says Nexus 3.70 is approved ... Authority(engineer,ArchitectureApproval)=False ... exactly the type of distinction a governance-aware KnowledgeOS needs
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: a technically reliable engineer's approval statement is Authority(engineer,ArchitectureApproval)=False since only the Architecture Board can authorize — technically useful evidence can be insufficient for authoritative approval.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(H\mid E) ... not Reliability(E), nor Authority(E), nor Confidence(E)
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Probability P(H|E) as uncertainty under an explicit probabilistic model, distinct from Reliability, Authority, and Confidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Confidence is unfortunately overloaded ... Confidence=(value,model,interpretation)
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes 'confidence' is overloaded (subjective/model/statistical-level/probability/classifier-score) and should never be stored as a bare number without a ConfidenceModel; proposes Confidence=(value,model,interpretation) if used at all.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_1 and E_2 both support H. We cannot simply assume E_1\perp E_2 ... need to examine their causal/provenance relationship
b_rows_sample.statement: States Independence as the most important statistical dimension: co-supporting evidence cannot be assumed independent without examining causal/provenance relationships.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Vendor document -> Human summary / LLM summary ... E_2=f(E_1), E_3=g(E_1) ... EvidenceCount\neq InformationCount
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked classic double-counting example: human and LLM summaries both derived from one vendor document are not independent observations — counting them as three sources falsely inflates support — 'EvidenceCount ≠ InformationCount,' called 'a fundamental principle.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: G_E=(V,E) ... nodes are evidence/artifacts and edges represent derivation/dependency ... allows us to detect obvious double-counting
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an evidence lineage graph G_E=(V,E) with nodes as evidence/artifacts and edges as derivation/dependency, illustrated with a vendor-document/human-extract/LLM-extract/assertion diagram, enabling double-counting detection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EvidenceClusters ... C_1=\{VendorDocument,HumanSummary,LLMSummary\} ... InformationUnits(C_1)\approx1 unless additional independent observations exist
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines EvidenceClusters grouping evidence sharing a common informational origin; a cluster contributes InformationUnits≈1 unless additional independent observations exist.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Production API->E1, Filesystem inspection->E2, Independent human inspection->E3 ... E_1\perp E_2 may be justified ... based on the actual acquisition mechanism, not simply they came from different people
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts genuinely independent acquisition paths (API, filesystem inspection, independent human inspection), warning independence must be justified by acquisition mechanism, not merely 'different people.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_1\perp E_2\mid H ... ConditionalIndependence(E_1,E_2\mid H,C) ... should not force everything into simple binary independence
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces conditional independence E1⊥E2|H, generalized to ConditionalIndependence(E1,E2|H,C), avoiding forcing evidence into simple binary independence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Polarity(E,H)\in\{Positive,Negative,Neutral,Unknown\} ... a useful deterministic layer before probabilistic aggregation
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines evidence Polarity(E,H) in {Positive,Negative,Neutral,Unknown}, a deterministic layer applied before any probabilistic aggregation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Strength(E,H) ... LikelihoodRatio\gg1 ... LikelihoodRatio\approx1 ... statistically meaningful measure of evidential strength may be a likelihood ratio, not a subjective score
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues evidential Strength(E,H) is best captured by a likelihood ratio rather than a subjective score, contrasting strong (LR>>1) vs weak (LR≈1) measurements.

b_rows_sample.anchor: LR(E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)}{P(E\mid\neg H)} ... LR>1 favors H, LR<1 favors \neg H, LR\approx1 little discrimination ... much more principled than Confidence=0.8
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines the likelihood ratio LR(E)=P(E|H)/P(E|¬H) with a three-way interpretation (favors H, favors ¬H, uninformative), 'much more principled than Confidence=0.8.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: LR(E_1,E_2)=LR(E_1)\cdot LR(E_2) ... LR(E_1,\ldots,E_n)=\prod_i LR(E_i) under the appropriate independence assumptions
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines combination of conditionally independent evidence via multiplied likelihood ratios: LR(E1,...,En)=prod LR(Ei), 'a mathematically valid evidence-combination mechanism.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: No independence assumption without provenance/model justification
b_rows_sample.statement: States the strict invariant that the LR product formula must never be applied automatically without provenance/model justification for E_i⊥E_j|H — otherwise 'severe overconfidence' results.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Odds(H)=P(H)/(1-P(H)) ... Odds(H\mid E)=Odds(H)\times LR(E) ... requires a valid prior; valid likelihoods; a valid dependency model. Without those, we should not fabricate probabilities
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Bayesian odds updating Odds(H|E)=Odds(H)*LR(E), generalized to independent multi-evidence updating, with an explicit requirement for a valid prior/likelihoods/dependency model — otherwise probabilities must not be fabricated.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'evidence-aggregation-heterogeneous-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'evidence-aggregation-algebra' (batch B0022). Note: S0907's Step 25N: the fully worked statistical/qualitative evidence-aggregation model (likelihood ratios, evidence clusters, authority-vs-reliability separation, no-universal-aggregation-function conclusion); extends B0021's evidence-aggregation-axioms (S0859) and S0892's evidence-aggregation-algebra (B0021) with a concrete operator, DDD service mapping, and eight falsification tests.
working_label token overlap Jaccard=0.75 (shared tokens: ['aggregation', 'algebra', 'evidence'])

a_rows_sample.anchor: def SI(K, C, T, critical, declared_loss): ... 8 executed cases
a_rows_sample.statement: Executed deterministic Python implementation of Step 222's SI(T,K,C) definition, run against all 8 scenarios mandated by the verification directive (complete preservation, partial loss undeclared, partial loss declared, AI-summary case matching SS222.14, empty critical set, contradictory declaration, ambiguous context A/B); cases 1-4 behave correctly, matching the corpus's own stated expectations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CriticalSemantics(K,C) = \emptyset \Rightarrow SI = 1 for ANY transformation, including one that destroys everything.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defect 1 (VACUOUS SATISFACTION, case 5): SI has no non-triviality condition on the critical-semantics set -- if CriticalSemantics(K,C) is empty, any transformation (including one that destroys everything) scores SI=1, since the declarer controls what counts as critical; identified as the same defect class as Step 100's vacuous closure theorem (TV-F-045, a universally-quantified condition over a possibly-empty set).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Declaring loss of an attribute the transform actually preserves returns SI = 1 with no complaint. ... A declarer may over-declare freely
a_rows_sample.statement: Defect 2 (INCOHERENT DECLARATIONS UNDETECTED, case 6): the definition never checks DeclaredLoss against what was actually lost, so a declarer may freely over-declare loss and still pass, weakening the audit value of the declaration mechanism itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Identical K, identical T, two contexts => SI flips from 1 to 0. ... one may never say 'T preserves semantic integrity'. Only 'T preserves SI relative to C' is meaningful.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defect 3 (SI IS A TERNARY RELATION, case 7): identical K and T under two different contexts flip SI from 1 to 0 -- correct by design (SI is context-relative) but with an architectural consequence the corpus does not observe: unqualified claims of the form 'T preserves semantic integrity' (found at SS218.31's Semantic Preservation Principle, SS219.25, and SS222.36's verdict, none naming C) are not well-formed under SI's own definition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: SI(T1)=1 (declared Confidence) ... SI(T2)=1 (declared Source) ... SI(T2 \circ T1)=0 L={Confidence,Source} -> undeclared. ... Each stage individually satisfies semantic integrity. The composite does not.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defect 4 (COMPOSITION FAILS -- the decisive result): a constructed counterexample with T1 (drops Confidence, declares it) and T2 (drops Source, declares it) each individually satisfy SI=1, but the composite T2 o T1 scores SI=0 because the corpus defines no composition rule for DeclaredLoss (it would need to union under composition); this matters because the corpus's own stated motivating case -- the AI pipeline Input->Interpretation->Summary->Recommendation (SS218.32, SS219.22) -- is exactly such a multi-stage composition, so SI as defined cannot evaluate the pipeline it was written to govern. The failure mode is identified as an instance of the corpus's own oldest theorem LocalCorrectness not-implies GlobalCorrectness (boxed at step-048 SS48.1, step-058 SS58.3, and steps 091/208/211 -- five prior boxings, none cited by Step 222's SI.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Well-typed YES ... Decidable YES ... Falsifiable YES ... Useful PARTIALLY ... Stable under composition NO -- REFUTED BY EXECUTED COUNTEREXAMPLE.
a_rows_sample.statement: Part 1 verdict table for SI: Well-typed YES (genuine improvement on SS215.10's ill-typed proportional-to), Decidable YES given finite CriticalSemantics/Recoverable sets, Falsifiable YES (cases 2 and 4 correctly return 0), Useful PARTIALLY (correct on design cases but vacuously satisfiable when critical=empty), Stable under composition NO (refuted by executed counterexample) -- overall: SI is a real improvement and genuine repair of TV-F-083, but incomplete in a way that defeats its own motivating use case.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ESTABLISHED: 1. SI is well-typed, decidable and falsifiable ... NOT ESTABLISHED: that SI is useful at scale; that Recoverable(T(K)) is computable for real transformations ... that any declaration of CriticalSemantics exists anywhere in the corpus for any real artifact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Part 3 summary of what this executed test establishes: (1) SI is well-typed/decidable/falsifiable -- TV-F-083 genuinely repaired; (2) SI is vacuously satisfiable when CriticalSemantics=empty; (3) SI does not compose, refuted by explicit counterexample, the failure being the corpus's own uncited LocalCorrectness-not-implies-GlobalCorrectness theorem; (4) SI is a ternary relation, so unqualified 'T preserves semantic integrity' statements are not well-formed; (5) conditional invariants dissolve two MCS, not four, MCS-2 survives, MCS-4 is relocated not resolved. Explicitly NOT established: that SI is useful at scale, that Recoverable(T(K)) is computable for real transformations (the finite-set case tested here is the favorable case), or that any real corpus artifact has ever actually declared a CriticalSemantics set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Add a composition rule: DeclaredLoss(T2 \circ T1) \supseteq DeclaredLoss(T1) \cup DeclaredLoss(T2). Executed test confirms this restores SI = 1 for the counterexample.
a_rows_sample.statement: Part 4 (verifier-recommended, not applied, evidence class E): five possible repairs -- (1) a composition rule DeclaredLoss(T2 o T1) superset-or-equal union of DeclaredLoss(T1),DeclaredLoss(T2), executed-tested to confirm it restores SI=1 for the counterexample, rated the highest-leverage fix since without it SI cannot evaluate the AI pipeline it exists to govern; (2) a non-triviality condition barring CriticalSemantics=empty or requiring the empty declaration to be justified; (3) requiring DeclaredLoss subseteq L so over-declaration is detected; (4) always writing SI(T,K,C) with C explicit, retiring unqualified 'preserves semantic integrity' claims; (5) declaring the projection pi for MCS-1, specifying the partial order for MCS-4, naming the entropy for MCS-5, and declaring an enumerable Q for MCS-2 -- none of these repairs is established by the corpus itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: For every candidate principle P, define: $$F(P)=\{\text{observations that would contradict }P\}.$$ ... We must not use "Supported" merely because we can find examples that fit.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 establishes its falsification rule: for every candidate principle P, define F(P) as the set of observations that would contradict it, search the historical material for those observations, and classify the result as Supported/Partially Supported/Contradicted/Undetermined -- explicitly forbidding calling a principle Supported merely because confirming examples can be found.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Even if some implementation violates this principle, that does **not** automatically disprove the architectural principle. It may instead establish: $$Architecture_{intended}\neq Architecture_{implemented}.$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's falsification test for Identity!=State notes that an implementation violation does not automatically disprove the architectural principle -- it may instead establish Architecture_intended != Architecture_implemented, which must be recorded as its own distinct finding.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If the system deliberately defines observations and interpretations as the same semantic object, with no distinction required by any use case, then this principle may be too strong. The correct conclusion might instead be: $$Observation\approx Interpretation$$ within a specific bounded context.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's falsification test for Observation!=Interpretation allows for the principle to be contextually weakened rather than outright rejected: if no use case requires the distinction in some bounded context, the correct conclusion is Observation approximately Interpretation within that specific context, not universal rejection of the distinction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: But if missing evidence is repeatedly converted into negative conclusions, we have evidence of **epistemic collapse**.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's falsification test for Unknown!=False names 'epistemic collapse' as the failure pattern where missing evidence is repeatedly converted into negative conclusions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We should search Steps 1–182 for cases where knowledge itself is intentionally defined as sufficient authority. ... The correct model may be: $$Authority=f(Context,Role,Policy).$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's falsification test for Knowledge!=Authority proposes that if a counterexample domain exists where knowledge is intentionally sufficient authority, the distinction should not be universalized; the correct model would instead be Authority=f(Context,Role,Policy).

b_rows_sample.anchor: If a bounded context explicitly models autonomous action ... then the distinction may be unnecessary **inside that context**. But at governance level, the distinction may still be required. Thus: $$LocalSemantics\neq GovernanceSemantics.$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's falsification test for Decision!=Execution introduces LocalSemantics!=GovernanceSemantics: a distinction unnecessary inside one bounded context's autonomous-action model may still be required at the governance level, meaning distinctions can be context-scoped rather than universal.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This should almost certainly survive. $$\boxed{Implemented\neq Verified}$$ A line of code is not an assurance argument. ... A test that passes is not automatically proof of the complete invariant.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 judges Implementation!=Verification as the candidate principle most likely to survive falsification, reiterating that a passing test is not automatically proof of a complete invariant.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Now we attack the strongest candidate. $$\boxed{SemanticIntegrity}$$ ... could potentially explain the majority of architectural decisions without semantic integrity being central. If so, Semantic Integrity should **not** become the central architectural thesis.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 subjects Semantic Integrity, the strongest candidate central concept, to falsification by naming rival explanations (Performance, Scalability, Security, OrganizationalPolitics) that, if they better explain the majority of Steps 1-182's architectural decisions, would mean Semantic Integrity should not become the central architectural thesis.

b_rows_sample.anchor: $$Coverage(P)=\frac{\text{independent historical problems explained by }P}{\text{major historical problems examined}}.$$ Not necessarily as a literal numerical statistic. It is an audit measure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 defines Coverage(P) as a conceptual (not necessarily literal numerical) audit measure of how many independent historical problems a candidate principle explains, without being artificially stretched.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A weak theory can explain anything because it is too vague. ... $$\boxed{A\ good\ architectural\ principle\ must\ exclude\ something.}$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 states an anti-vacuity falsifiability principle: a good architectural principle must exclude something, explicitly warning against theories (like 'everything is about semantic integrity') becoming unfalsifiable through over-broad definition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate definition: A transformation preserves semantic integrity if all distinctions required by the receiving context ... remain recoverable or their loss is explicitly declared. ... This gives the concept a falsifiable form. $$SI(T,K,C)=1$$ if: $$CriticalSemantics(K,C)\subseteq Recoverable(T(K))$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 operationalizes Semantic Integrity into a falsifiable Boolean predicate SI(T,K,C): 1 if all context-critical semantics remain recoverable after transformation T or their loss is explicitly declared, 0 otherwise -- explicitly designed to give the concept testable, falsifiable form.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If: $$Observation$$ and: $$Inference$$ are indistinguishable in S, then: $$L\neq\varnothing.$$ If that distinction matters to the receiving context: $$SI=0.$$ This is a concrete architectural failure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's worked AI-summarization example (K={Observation,Inference,Confidence,Source,Time} compressed to S={Conclusion}) shows the operationalized SI predicate correctly flagging semantic loss (Observation/Inference conflation) as a concrete architectural failure when the distinction matters to the receiving context.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose: $$Decision=(Authority,Policy,Scope,Time,Reason).$$ The implementation stores only: approved = true ... The database may be technically correct. Yet: $$SI=0.$$ This is exactly why data integrity and semantic integrity are different.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's worked governance example shows a Decision 5-tuple (Authority,Policy,Scope,Time,Reason) collapsed in implementation to a single Boolean 'approved=true' field, correctly flagged by the SI predicate as semantic integrity failure (SI=0) despite technical database correctness -- illustrating the Data-Integrity vs Semantic-Integrity distinction concretely.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose: $$P(H|E)=0.68.$$ A transformation writes: H = true ... The transformation has changed: $$ProbabilisticClaim\rightarrow CategoricalFact.$$ That is semantic loss.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222's worked statistical-inference example shows a probabilistic claim P(H|E)=0.68 collapsed by a transformation into a categorical fact 'H=true', explicitly named as semantic loss (ProbabilisticClaim->CategoricalFact).

b_rows_sample.anchor: The model: $$F_\theta$$ and the empirical evidence: $$\hat F_n$$ must not be conflated. Thus: $$\boxed{Model\neq Observation.}$$ This is mathematically analogous to: $$Interpretation\neq Observation.$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 connects the empirical-vs-theoretical distribution (F_theta the model, F-hat_n the empirical CDF) to the Model!=Observation principle, drawn as mathematically analogous to the architectural Interpretation!=Observation distinction, giving the mathematical architecture explanatory rather than merely decorative status.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We should **not** say: "Architecture can always be measured with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic." That would be mathematically unjustified. The legitimate correspondence is: $$StatisticalModelValidation\sim ArchitecturalModelValidation$$ at the level of reasoning pattern.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 explicitly warns against overclaiming a specific statistical technique's (Kolmogorov-Smirnov) universal applicability to architecture validation, restricting the legitimate correspondence to the level of reasoning pattern (StatisticalModelValidation similar-to ArchitecturalModelValidation), with the specific mathematical technique requiring separate justification per application.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The stronger question is: **Does the engineering concept independently exist, and does the Gītā reflection illuminate it without becoming its alleged source?** Therefore: $$EngineeringOrigin$$ must remain independently traceable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 states the correct falsification question for Gita correspondences is not whether a similar-sounding verse can be found, but whether the engineering concept independently exists with the Gita illuminating rather than originating it -- EngineeringOrigin must remain independently traceable.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We should preserve the distinction: ### P1 — Historical influence ... ### P2 — Explicit interpretive analogy ... ### P3 — Retrospective resonance ... This is legitimate, but should be labeled exactly that.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 restates and applies the P1/P2/P3 philosophical-relationship taxonomy (historical influence, explicit interpretive analogy, retrospective resonance) originating in Step 216, requiring each to be evidenced and labeled exactly as what it is.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We should not treat P3 as inferior merely because it is retrospective. A retrospective correspondence can reveal: $$StructuralIsomorphism$$ ... But it must not be rewritten as: $$HistoricalCausation.$$ That would distort the history.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 argues P3 (retrospective philosophical resonance) is not inferior merely for being retrospective -- it can reveal genuine structural isomorphism between domains -- but explicitly warns it must never be rewritten as historical causation, which would distort the record.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Do **not** fill the unknown cells from intuition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 222 presents an unfilled philosophical evidence matrix (Gita chapter x technical candidate x independent engineering evidence x P1/P2/P3 relation x confidence) with all cells left as '?' and an explicit instruction not to fill them from intuition, deferring population to the actual historical audit.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
Logical omniscience: The system believes all logical consequences ... computationally intractable and cognitively unrealistic. ... four-valued situations: True only, False only, Both, Neither. ... Beliefs are not closed under implication. ... {Bp,B(p\supset q),
eg Bq} ... {Bp,B
eg p,
eg Bq} inconsistent beliefs without omniscience
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces the B (explicit belief) operator using four-valued situations (true-only/false-only/both/neither) to avoid logical omniscience -- beliefs are not closed under implication or consequence, exemplified by satisfiable sets {Bp,B(p⊃q),¬Bq} and inconsistent-without-explosion {Bp,B¬p,¬Bq}; a first-order variant interprets existential quantification constructively, making existential generalization fail (not |= B(P(a)∨P(b))⊃B∃xP(x)); complexity results range from co-NP-complete (propositional) to undecidable (first-order with existential generalization).

type_signature.domain: formula phi, epistemic state e, situation s

a_rows_sample.anchor: EOC = Explicit Only-knowing with Complete introspection ... Mark terms that appear within modal operators with triangle. Teach(father(tom),sara)\land\neg B Teach(father(tom)^\triangle,sara) ... Decidability: first-order with unrestricted equality Undecidable.
a_rows_sample.statement: EOC logic extends B with nested beliefs, only-knowing, and equality, introducing a triangle-marking device to solve quantifying-in with explicit belief (marking terms evaluated at substitution time versus modal-operator time); catalogues decidability results ranging from O(nm) propositional to undecidable first-order-with-unrestricted-equality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Recommendation: Integrate the book's findings into KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2, particularly: 1. The TELL/ASK framework -> Core operations 2. The Representation Theorem -> Sat semantics 3. Only-knowing -> Zero definition 4. Explicit belief (B) -> Tractable reasoning 5. Successor state axioms -> delta semantics 6. The triangle operator -> Quantifying-in with explicit belief

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contr: Four-valued semantics handles contradiction without collapse. We should mark this SUPPORTING EVIDENCE ONLY. ... our own KR-CONTR-FDE experiments already showed FDE is insufficient by itself. ... Four-valued belief \neq Contr and B/N \neq Zero remain intact.

b_rows_sample.anchor: pickingUp(x,do(c,s))\equiv startPickup(x)\in c\lor(pickingUp(x,s)\land endPickup(x)\notin c) ... Poss(startMoveLeft,s)\equiv\neg movingLeft(s) ... Poss(\{startMoveLeft,startMoveRight\},s) should be false. The converse of the foundational axiom need not hold.
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends successor-state semantics to concurrent action sets (successor-state axiom for a concurrent-action fluent), and identifies the 'precondition interaction problem': individually-possible concurrent actions (startMoveLeft, startMoveRight) can be jointly impossible even though each satisfies its own precondition axiom, requiring additional interaction constraints beyond the individual precondition axioms.

b_rows_sample.anchor: [EXT] throughout. Extracted, not endorsed. ... The induction axiom is second-order. The extraction states the consequence plainly: the system is not fully first-order decidable. Any transfer inherits this. ... It rests on the causal completeness assumption ... This is an assumption about the axiomatiser's knowledge, not a theorem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates Reiter's formal ontology and axioms (already captured in S2536) under an explicit [EXT]/'extracted not endorsed' framing, emphasizing two carried-forward limitations for any KnowledgeOS transfer: the induction axiom is second-order (not fully first-order decidable), and the successor-state axiom rests on an unproven causal-completeness ASSUMPTION about the axiomatiser's own knowledge, not a theorem.

b_rows_sample.anchor: "conflicting_effects_from_F_false": ["F"], "conflicting_effects_from_F_true": ["F"], "conflict_resolved_silently_in_favour_of_gamma_plus": true, "finding": "when gamma+ and gamma- both name F, the SSA yields F TRUE with no signal that the effect axioms were inconsistent. The frame solution PRESUPPOSES consistent effect axioms; it does not detect their inconsistency."
b_rows_sample.statement: Executed result: a deliberately conflicting action (gamma+ and gamma- both naming fluent F) is silently resolved to F=TRUE from both prior states, with the successor-state axiom giving no signal that its own effect axioms were inconsistent -- confirming determinism and persistence-of-unmentioned-fluents work correctly, but exposing that inconsistency detection is entirely outside the mechanism's scope.

b_rows_sample.anchor: class Situation: """A situation IS a history: a finite sequence of actions.  NOT a state.""" ... def successor(self, a, state): """Successor state axiom:  F' = gamma+ ∨ (F ∧ ¬gamma-)""" ... def regress(self, fluent, sit): """REGRESSION: rewrite a query about sit into a query about S0, by unwinding the successor-state axiom backwards."""
b_rows_sample.statement: A minimal but faithful executable model of Reiter's situation calculus: a Situation as an immutable action tuple (explicitly a history, not a state), an ActionTheory with Poss/successor(SSA)/progress/executable/regress methods, used to generate all five A1-A5 experimental results in this batch; module docstring explicitly frames these as verification tests of Reiter's machinery, not a KnowledgeOS implementation, and states nothing here promotes any Reiter concept to a KnowledgeOS primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The METHOD transfers: "state what changes a thing; everything else persists by construction." This is genuinely useful and is the strongest positive result of this step.
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the frame-problem METHOD (specify only what changes; everything else persists by construction) as the single strongest positive, genuinely transferable result of the whole step-292 audit.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not confuse the observable representation with the underlying state. ... y_t = G(x_t) ... If G is not invertible, several underlying states can generate the same observation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Fraser's y_t=G(x_t) state-space formalization provides a mathematical version of 'language is a projection of meaning, not the container of meaning'; the research hypothesis becomes 'natural-language expressions may be observations generated by an underlying semantic/problem-solving state space', not word->meaning directly.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Fraser takes a quantized Lorenz dynamical system, gives an HMM only the observations, and trains it using Baum-Welch. The learned hidden states correspond approximately to regions of the original continuous state space.
a_rows_sample.statement: Cites Fraser's own Lorenz-system experiment (HMM trained only on quantized observations recovers approximate regions of the true continuous state space) as direct precedent supporting the plausibility of the batch's unsupervised latent-semantic-state discovery program.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Fraser applies an HMM to text and explicitly tries to discover parts of speech without supplying a dictionary or manually specifying the categories. ... many discovered hidden states correspond to recognizable grammatical categories.
a_rows_sample.statement: Called 'probably the strongest direct evidence for our direction': Fraser's own already-published experiment discovers grammatical parts-of-speech categories purely from raw tokenized text via HMM/Viterbi, without any supplied dictionary or category labels -- direct empirical precedent for the batch's proposed one-level-deeper semantic/operational-structure discovery.

a_rows_sample.anchor: An HMM can discover: grammatical states; stylistic states; author-specific states; topic states; formatting states; semantic states; domain states; accidental statistical clusters. Therefore: latent state != knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit warning that an HMM's discovered hidden state only indicates statistical structure representable by a hidden state, never automatically knowledge; other lenses (not-knowledge exclusion, invariance testing, ESL validation) must determine whether it qualifies.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Perhaps the fundamental unit isn't 'FILTER' but Z_i ->D-> Z_j, where D is a primitive transformation. ... UNKNOWN -> OBSERVE -> OBSERVED -> DIFFERENTIATE -> DISTINGUISHED -> SELECT -> CONSTRAINED. ... Dhatu a transition/operator rather than a semantic label.
a_rows_sample.statement: Central reframing hypothesis: the fundamental semantic primitive (dhatu) may be a state-transition operator (Z_i to Z_j via transformation D) rather than a noun-like semantic object, illustrated by an UNKNOWN->OBSERVE->OBSERVED->DIFFERENTIATE->DISTINGUISHED->SELECT->CONSTRAINED chain, explicitly said to fit the Paninian lens surprisingly well.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Baum-Welch can converge to different local maxima from different random initializations. ... A candidate semantic state must be stable across runs. ... This becomes one of our Shani invariants.
a_rows_sample.statement: Methodological warning generalized into a new Shani-level invariant: a candidate latent-state structure must remain stable across different Baum-Welch/EM random initializations before being accepted, since different runs can converge to different local optima.

a_rows_sample.anchor: an entropy gap as a measure of how faithfully a model represents the generating process. ... delta = model cross-entropy / process entropy. An ideal model has a gap approaching zero. This is very close to what we were looking for with Zero.
a_rows_sample.statement: Fraser's entropy-gap concept (ratio of model cross-entropy to process entropy, ideally approaching zero) proposed as yet another quantitative Zero criterion, combined with a formal (explicitly non-Fraser-attributed) Z*=argmin[Complexity(Z)+lambda*InformationLoss(Z)] optimization built from Fraser's ingredients (hidden-state representation, likelihood, entropy, cross-entropy, complexity, approximation error).

a_rows_sample.anchor: if observations do not uniquely determine the state, the state is hidden; but sufficiently informative sequences can sometimes identify the state. ... A candidate structure should not merely explain observations. It should be recoverable from observations sufficiently reliably.
a_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge-candidate identifiability criterion: test whether the posterior P(Z_t|Y_1..Y_T) becomes concentrated (less uncertain) as more evidence T accumulates; if it does, the latent state is identifiable; if not, the candidate structure may not be identifiable at all.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the Kalman filter alternates between forecasting the state distribution and updating it using the current observation. ... Predict -> Observe -> Update. Notice how this is not a noun. It is a transformation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Kalman filter's predict->observe->update cycle offered as a concrete candidate dhatu-as-operator example, reinforcing the transition-not-noun hypothesis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: optimizing likelihood and optimizing classification performance are not necessarily the same objective. ... latent state estimation != knowledge classification. ... 'The HMM found this state, therefore it found knowledge.' Instead: HMM -> latent structure candidate -> Zero tests -> invariance tests -> cross-domain tests -> ESL validation -> knowledge candidate.
a_rows_sample.statement: Estimation != Classification invariant, closing the full validation chain (HMM discovery -> Zero tests -> invariance tests -> cross-domain tests -> ESL validation -> knowledge candidate) that must be traversed before any discovered latent state is treated as knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge may be represented by a minimal, statistically recoverable latent dynamical structure whose predictive/explanatory behavior survives changes in observation representation. And consequently: Dhatu may be a minimal transition/operator in that latent state space rather than a minimal word, concept, or semantic object.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the file's central revised hypothesis, replacing the earlier 'knowledge consists of minimal semantic objects' hypothesis with 'knowledge is a minimal statistically-recoverable latent dynamical structure whose behavior survives representation changes', and dhatu specifically as a minimal transition/operator rather than a word/concept/object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment A - linguistic states ... Experiment B - semantic states ... Experiment C - operational states ... Experiment D - Zero ... Experiment E - Dhatu: Examine recurring transitions Z_i -> Z_j rather than merely recurring state labels.
a_rows_sample.statement: Complete five-part experiment design closing the four-book research program: A) recover grammatical/structural categories via HMM on tokens across diverse corpora (mathematics, science, philosophy, engineering, literature, Sanskrit grammar, problem-solving); B) discover stable semantic regimes via HMM on sentence-level semantic features; C) discover recurring operational trajectories (e.g. OBSERVE->DIFFERENTIATE->SELECT->ACT) in problem-solving text; D) sweep state count (2..64) measuring complexity/prediction/cross-entropy/stability/generalization to find minimum stable sufficient representation; E) examine recurring state-to-state transitions (not state labels) as candidate dhatu operators.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ESL teaches us how to measure, select, regularize and validate learned structure. PRML teaches us how to construct a probabilistic representation of hidden structure and reason through it.
b_rows_sample.statement: Assigns PRML a distinct scientific job (constructing/reasoning about latent probabilistic structure) complementary to ESL's validation role and Solution Mindset's observational role, completing a three-book research architecture.

b_rows_sample.anchor: introducing latent variables allows complicated observable distributions to be represented through simpler components in an expanded space ... we should not assume FILTER is a Dhatu. We should test whether multiple apparently different observations are better explained by a common latent structure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives 'dhatu' a mathematical interpretation as a latent variable generating diverse observable manifestations (e.g. FILTER generating select/reject/isolate), with the explicit methodological caution to test rather than assume that a candidate observable operation is a genuine latent dhatu.

b_rows_sample.anchor: L0 RAW ... L1 OBSERVABLE OPERATION ... L2 LATENT STRUCTURE ... L3 INVARIANT. Our original Zero Lens was mostly operating between L1 and L3. PRML gives us the missing machinery for L2.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes a four-layer representation hierarchy (Raw/Observable-Operation/Latent-Structure/Invariant), explicitly identifying that the prior Zero-Lens work skipped the L2 latent-structure layer, which PRML's machinery now fills.

b_rows_sample.anchor: a two-dimensional nonlinear manifold adjusted to the data, with observations mapped into latent space through posterior distributions. ... 500 observable concepts -> 80 operational features -> 12 latent dimensions -> 5 stable semantic axes. Those five axes may be more fundamental than any particular vocabulary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses PRML's nonlinear latent-variable family (GTM etc.) to argue the semantic space is unlikely to be purely linear, reframing the research question from 'what are the semantic primitives?' to 'what is the dimensionality and geometry of the latent semantic space?', illustrated with a worked reduction chain from 500 concepts to 5 stable semantic axes.

b_rows_sample.anchor: a way to ask: Which operations become irrelevant once certain information is known? ... the semantic system has information bottlenecks. This could potentially connect our Zero Lens to a formal notion of sufficient representation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses PRML's d-separation/conditional-independence framework to pose 'information bottleneck' questions for a theory of problem solving: which prior operations become conditionally irrelevant once a later state is known, connecting to a formal notion of sufficient representation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: introducing latent variables and then iteratively estimating their posterior responsibilities in the E-step and optimizing the expected complete-data log likelihood in the M-step. ... instead of manually defining the Dhatus first, we can potentially discover candidate latent operators iteratively.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes EM as an iterative latent-operator discovery loop (hypothesize latent operators -> infer assignments -> update operator model -> repeat), avoiding the need to manually define candidate dhatus in advance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Is human problem solving better represented as a static ontology of operations, or as a probabilistic dynamical system over latent semantic states? That is a much stronger scientific question.
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses the central alternative hypothesis: 'Problem = bag of operators' versus 'Problem = trajectory through latent states' (a Markov/HMM-style state-transition system), grounded in PRML's mixture-model->HMM/dynamical-system progression.

b_rows_sample.anchor: an Occam factor, explicitly penalizing unnecessarily complex models ... We don't want 1000 latent operators just because the model can fit everything. Nor do we want 3 universal operators because we imposed an aesthetic preference for simplicity. ... Zero becomes model selection, not merely philosophical reduction.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses PRML's Occam-factor/BIC model-evidence machinery to reformulate Zero once more: an optimal-complexity model selection problem, avoiding both overfitting (too many operators) and an aesthetically-imposed minimalism (too few), rather than pure philosophical reduction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can complex human reasoning be generated from a small compositional vocabulary of primitive operations? If yes, then we have something resembling a generative theory of problem solving.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the overarching hypothesis the whole three-book research program is testing: whether complex human problem-solving reasoning can be generated compositionally from a small vocabulary of primitive latent operations, amounting to a generative theory of problem solving.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would not proceed by reading all three books sequentially. Instead, I would build a cross-book operator matrix. ... The interesting result will not be whether the names match. It will be whether the structural signatures match.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a formal cross-book operator matrix (Concept, Primitive operation, Input, Transformation, Output, Assumption, Objective, Failure mode, Invariance, Latent/observable status, Temporal status, Validation mechanism) worked through a full example for EM, to compare PRML/ESL concepts against Solution Mindset operators by structural signature rather than superficial name matching -- named the genuinely interesting part of the experiment.
